checks.claim: Stem definition: renewable = nature replaces it within a human lifetime; nonrenewable = it does not
checks.note: National Geographic glossary: nonrenewable = 'exhaustible relative to the human life span'. Grokipedia Natural_resource: non-renewables 'cannot be regenerated on human timescales'.

checks.claim: Key: coal is nonrenewable and takes millions of years to form
checks.note: EIA: coal is nonrenewable 'because it takes millions of years to form'.

checks.claim: Oil and natural gas are likewise nonrenewable, formed over millions of years
checks.note: Fossil fuels formed 'over millions of years'; gas, coal, petroleum named as nonrenewable.

checks.claim: Wrong choice Firewood: renewable (wood is biomass)
checks.note: EIA lists biomass, including 'Wood and wood waste', as renewable. Not defensible as nonrenewable under the stem's definition.

checks.claim: Context: new trees grow back in 20 to 100 years
checks.note: Grokipedia table: 'tree regrowth: 20-100 years'. Within (or close to) a human lifetime, so firewood fits the stem's definition.

checks.claim: Context: a forest can still run out if cut faster than it regrows
checks.note: Renewables are 'vulnerable to overexploitation when human demands surpass replenishment'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices Wind and Sunlight: renewable, not used up by use
checks.note: EIA: renewable sources are 'naturally replenishing but flow-limited' and 'virtually inexhaustible'.

checks.claim: Copper wire can be melted down and remade; recycled copper is as good as new
checks.note: International Copper Association: copper 'can be used again and again without losing any of its properties' and recycled copper 'can be used in exactly the same way as newly mined copper'. Industry source, but uncontested.

checks.claim: Key: copper is nonrenewable because nature makes new ore far too slowly
checks.note: Grokipedia: ores' finite nature stems from 'the irreplaceable geological timescales required for their formation', processes operating 'over millions of years'. The reasoning (renewable vs nonrenewable is about nature's replacement rate, not recyclability) is stated correctly.

checks.claim: Context: nature takes millions of years to make new ore
checks.note: Acceptable. Nuance: porphyry deposits (the 'dominant source of copper that is mined today') form 1-6 km down; geochronology dates their ore-forming pulses at tens of thousands to a few million years (SEG 2017 abstract, Heinrich/von Quadt; Virmond et al. 2024), and exposing them takes millions of years of uplift and erosion. Grokipedia says 'over millions of years'. Optional softer wording: 'nature takes many thousands to millions of years to make new ore'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: copper wears out after being recycled a few times
checks.note: False: copper keeps its properties through repeated recycling.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: copper is made in factories, not by nature
checks.note: False: copper is mined from natural ore deposits; refining purifies it but does not make it.

checks.claim: Wrong choice / context: copper does not rust; it grows a thin protective green coat
checks.note: Grokipedia: copper's 'non-ferrous nature prevents rusting'; it forms 'a protective patina over time'; verdigris-patina roofs have lasted over 100 years. Rust is iron oxide.

checks.claim: Context: copper is nonrenewable like other metals and most minerals
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'Mineral and metal ores represent non-renewable resources'.

checks.claim: Stem: topsoil forms from weathered rock grains plus rotting plant and animal matter
checks.note: Grokipedia: weathering of parent material, and 'decomposition of plant residues and animal matter'.

checks.claim: Key: about 2.5 cm of topsoil usually takes hundreds of years
checks.note: Montgomery (Scientific American): 300-850 years per inch at Heimsath's sites, 700-1,500 years in a global compilation. Grokipedia: 500-1,000 years per 2.5 cm. Tropical soils faster (~150-200 years), deserts thousands; 'hundreds of years' is the safe usual figure.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'About twenty years'
checks.note: Wrong for natural formation. Closest outlier found: Iowa State Extension says about 30 years to develop 1 inch 'with properties of typical topsoil' in Iowa's deep, permeable soils (an agronomic soil-loss-tolerance figure, not formation from rock). Still not twenty, and the stem asks what nature usually takes, so the choice stays wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong choices 'About two years', 'A few months'
checks.note: Far too fast for any measured natural rate (Grokipedia: 0.01-1 mm per year).

checks.claim: Context: about 2.5 cm takes roughly 500 to 1,000 years under natural conditions
checks.note: Grokipedia ('2.5 cm ... may require 500 to 1,000 years') and Wikipedia agree. Some field studies are faster (300 years) and some slower (1,500), so 'roughly' is needed; optional widening: 'a few hundred to a thousand years or more'.

checks.claim: Context: rain and wind often carry topsoil away faster than it forms
checks.note: Grokipedia: erosion removes topsoil 'at rates often exceeding formation'.

checks.claim: Key: most plastic is made from oil and natural gas
checks.note: EIA: plastics are 'produced from natural gas, feedstocks derived from natural gas processing' and from crude-oil refining. Grokipedia Plastic: 'natural gas and crude oil derivatives like ethylene and propylene'. Pairing both fuels is right (in the US natural gas is the main feedstock).

checks.claim: Context: over 90 percent of plastic is made from fossil fuels
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'over 90% of plastics originate from fossil-based petrochemicals'. Plastics Europe Fast Facts 2024: fossil-based 90.4% of 413.8 Mt in 2023 (most of the rest is recycled plastic, itself originally fossil). Holds; it sits close to 90, so 'about 90 percent' would be more durable if recycling grows.

checks.claim: Context: less than 1 percent comes from plants
checks.note: Plastics Europe: bio-based and bio-attributed plastics 0.6% of global production in 2024 (0.7% in 2023). Grokipedia: bioplastics 'less than 1%'.

checks.claim: Context: 'mostly oil and natural gas' (other fossil fuels exist)
checks.note: Correct as 'mostly': some plastic is made from coal (e.g. coal-to-olefins in China), which the wording leaves room for.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: wood and plant fibres (they make paper)
checks.note: Paper is made of cellulose fibres from wood pulp. A few plastics are cellulose-based, but under 1% of plastic is plant-based, so not 'most'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: sand and limestone (they make glass)
checks.note: Soda-lime glass, nearly 90% of all glass, is silica sand, soda ash and limestone; 'sand and limestone are melted into glass' is a fair simplification.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: sap from rubber trees (makes natural rubber)
checks.note: Grokipedia: natural rubber is 'a milky white latex emulsion from the bark of the Pará rubber tree', and calls it 'latex sap'. Rubber is not plastic.

checks.claim: Stem: aluminium for cans can come from bauxite, a mined rock, or from melted old cans
checks.note: Bauxite is the primary ore; used beverage cans are remelted into new can sheet.

checks.claim: Key: recycling saves almost all of the energy (about 95 percent; about 5 percent of the energy needed)
checks.note: International Aluminium Institute: recycling saves 95% (8.3 GJ/t vs primary; 95.5%). Aluminum Association (aluminum.org/Recycling): 95%. Grokipedia Aluminium_recycling: 'merely 5% of the energy'. An older DOE figure via EIA says 90%; either way 'almost all' holds.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: about half, about a tenth, none
checks.note: All far below the measured 90-95%.

checks.claim: Context: each tonne of recycled aluminium leaves about four tonnes of bauxite in the ground
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'recycling one tonne of aluminum conserves approximately four tonnes of bauxite ore' (primary production uses roughly 4-6 t of ore per t).

checks.claim: Context: aluminium can be recycled over and over without wearing out
checks.note: Standard claim (Aluminum Association: 'infinitely recyclable'; Grokipedia: 'indefinite recyclability without loss of quality'). Grokipedia notes a caveat: alloy impurities (iron, silicon) build up in mixed scrap, so some is blended with new metal; the can-to-can loop is the cleanest case. Fine at grade 5.

checks.claim: Key: paper is the listed material that wears out with recycling (fibres shorten and weaken)
checks.note: Grokipedia: pulping and refining 'shorten fiber length'; fines and hornification weaken it; virgin fibre must be blended in. Paper is the only one of the four choices that degrades.

checks.claim: Stem 'only a few times' and context 'after about five to seven times new fibres must be mixed in'
checks.note: The 5-7 figure is the long-standing consensus (archived EPA papermaking page: 'generally accepted' a fibre can be used five to seven times; Grokipedia: 4-7 or 5-7 cycles). But a 2021 Graz University of Technology lab study (Dr Rene Eckhart, industry-commissioned) ran cartonboard through 25 recycling loops and found no negative effect on strength, calling the 4-7 figure a myth. Not peer-reviewed in what I found, and the key still stands as the only material that degrades. Fix: stem 'Which material wears out a little each time it is recycled?'; context 'so in the end new fibres must be mixed in (often said to be after about five to seven times, though a 2021 test of cardboard found its fibres still strong after 25)'. Or keep as is if the lead accepts the older consensus.

checks.claim: Wrong choice Glass: can be recycled again and again without wearing out
checks.note: BCG/Glass Packaging Institute: glass is 'infinitely recyclable ... without a loss in quality or purity'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice Aluminium: recycled again and again without wearing out
checks.note: Aluminum Association: infinitely recyclable (alloy-impurity caveat noted under the aluminium question; does not make it wear out after a few times).

checks.claim: Wrong choice Steel: recycled again and again without wearing out
checks.note: AISC: structural steel recycled 'with no loss of its physical properties'; Eurofer: recyclable 'over and over again in a closed loop'; worldsteel: recycled steel keeps its properties.

checks.claim: Context: paper is made of tiny wood fibres
checks.note: Cellulose fibres from wood pulp.

checks.claim: Key: filling an empty jam jar with buttons is reusing
checks.note: Grokipedia: reuse is using an item again 'either in its original form or repurposed for a new function', with repurposed glass jars as an example; it keeps 'the item's integrity'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: melting old jars into new ones is recycling
checks.note: Recycling breaks the material down through industrial processes into new goods; not reuse.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: switching off lights in empty rooms is reducing
checks.note: Energy.gov: turn lights off when they are not needed to save electricity. Using less is reducing, not reuse.

checks.claim: Wrong choice / context: putting apple cores on a compost heap is recycling
checks.note: EPA classes composting as organics recycling (aerobic decomposition into soil amendment). The core is broken down, so it is not reuse.

checks.claim: Key: fixing a dripping tap, showering instead of bathing and sweeping steps instead of hosing are conserving water
checks.note: EPA WaterSense: fix leaks; 'Showers use less water than baths' (if kept short); 'Sweep driveways, sidewalks, and steps rather than hosing off'.

checks.claim: Context: conserving means using less and wasting less
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'the deliberate reduction of water consumption and waste'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices Recycling / Reusing: none of the jobs uses the same water twice
checks.note: Correct: nothing is used again or reprocessed.

checks.claim: Wrong choice Replenishing; context: nature replenishes fresh water through the water cycle
checks.note: The family adds no water; Grokipedia Renewable_resource lists 'freshwater from hydrological cycles' as replenished.

checks.claim: Key: a plastic bag left in a field breaks into tiny bits of plastic
checks.note: Grokipedia: weathering and UV 'do not eliminate the polymer but convert macroplastics into smaller fragments'; Plastic_pollution: 'fragment slowly over centuries without fully biodegrading'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: it rots away like a fallen leaf; context: bacteria and fungi break down almost no plastic
checks.note: Conventional plastics decompose 'primarily through abiotic mechanisms ... rather than biological breakdown under typical natural conditions'. Even bioplastics 'do not reliably decompose without controlled aerobic conditions'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: it slowly dissolves away in the rain
checks.note: Polyethylene bags are insoluble in water; they fragment, not dissolve.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: it burns away to nothing in the sun
checks.note: Sunlight photodegrades (breaks chains, causes brittleness); no combustion, no 'full mineralization'.

checks.claim: Context: sunlight makes it brittle; bits last decades or centuries
checks.note: UV causes 'brittleness'; polyethylene half-lives '50 to 1200 years in natural settings'; Plastic_pollution: 'decades to centuries'.

checks.claim: Context: the bits turn up in soil, air and the sea
checks.note: Microplastics in farmland soil, carried globally in air, and in ocean waters.

checks.claim: Context: more than 700 kinds of animals have been found to swallow plastic, mistaking it for food
checks.note: Kühn and van Franeker 2020 (Marine Pollution Bulletin): 701 marine species recorded ingesting debris (914 affected counting entanglement); land and freshwater species add more, so 'more than 700' holds. Grokipedia Plastic_pollution: 'Over 700 species'; 'Ingestion occurs when animals mistake plastics for food'. Slight overgeneralisation: some animals swallow it by accident while filter-feeding or inside prey; 'often mistaking it for food' would be more exact.

unit_notes: 8 ok, 1 uncertain, 0 errors. The one uncertain item is paper's 'five to seven times' limit: a 2021 Graz University of Technology lab study (industry-commissioned) found cartonboard fibres held up through 25 recycling loops; the key still stands, but softening 'only a few times' would future-proof it. Optional polish (not errors): copper ore 'millions of years' could read 'thousands to millions of years'; topsoil '500 to 1,000 years' could widen to 'a few hundred to a thousand years or more'; plastic ingestion 'mistaking it for food' could read 'often mistaking it for food'. Aluminium's 95 percent energy saving is confirmed by the International Aluminium Institute and the Aluminum Association (an older DOE figure says 90 percent; 'almost all' holds either way).
